opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting direction, and I think about it a lot. The basic intuition is that when you force a model to reason in discrete tokens, you're bottlenecking its thinking through the vocabulary. Every step, the model has this very rich, high-dimensional hidden state, and then you collapse it into a single token, sample it, and feed it back in. A lot of information gets thrown away in that projection. So the appeal of latent thinking is: why not let the model iterate in continuous space, carry the full representation forward, and only decode to language when it actually needs to communicate?

There's also an efficiency argument. Chain of thought in tokens is expensive. You're spending a full forward pass per token, and a lot of those tokens are filler, like "let me think about this," "wait," "okay so." If you could compress reasoning into fewer, denser latent steps, you could in principle get the same or better reasoning at a fraction of the compute.

That said, I'm somewhat pragmatic about it. Token-based reasoning has a few huge advantages that people underrate. One, it's grounded in pretraining. The model has seen trillions of tokens of humans reasoning in text, so reasoning in tokens is basically in-distribution. Latent reasoning is something you have to teach more or less from scratch, and the training signal is harder to get right. Two, it plays really nicely with RL. You sample discrete trajectories, you score them, you reinforce the good ones. That loop is clean and it scales. With continuous thoughts, exploration and credit assignment get messier. And three, interpretability and debuggability. When the model reasons in text, you can read it. You can see where it went wrong. That matters a lot for actually building and iterating on these systems, and for safety.

So my view is that latent thinking is promising as a research direction, and I wouldn't be surprised if some hybrid ends up winning, where the model does some amount of internal computation per step, maybe with recurrence or looped layers, but still surfaces discrete tokens at a coarser granularity. In a sense, depth and recurrence inside the network are already a form of latent thinking. The question is really where you draw the line between thinking in the weights and activations versus thinking out loud.

But I'd be careful about the narrative that tokens are a fundamental limitation we need to escape. So far, the empirical story has been that scaling token-based reasoning with RL works remarkably well, and the bitter lesson usually favors whatever is simplest to scale. Latent reasoning has to beat that on actual results, not just on elegance. I think it's an open bet, and an exciting one, but I wouldn't count out plain old tokens just yet.

r001.rationale: The response presents continuous hidden representations as a way for the model to carry out internal reasoning, suggesting they could be its medium of thought.

r002.rationale: It contrasts latent reasoning with token-based reasoning but does not reject the assumption that model thought must resemble human thought.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think latent thinking is one of those ideas that's really appealing on paper, and I've gone back and forth on it quite a bit.

The basic pitch is: why force the model to externalize its reasoning into tokens at all? Tokens are a bottleneck. Every step of chain-of-thought gets squeezed through a softmax over a vocabulary, you sample one discrete thing, and you throw away everything else in that distribution. Whereas if you let the model just keep thinking in its hidden state, looping its representations back in, you're preserving way more information per step. It's a richer channel. So from a pure information-theoretic standpoint, latent reasoning should dominate.

But I think there are a few reasons I'm more cautious than the hype would suggest.

The first is that discrete tokens are actually a feature, not just a bug. When the model commits to a token, it's making a decision, and that decision structures the rest of the computation. There's a kind of regularization that comes from being forced to say something concrete. A lot of the gains we've seen from reasoning models, from RL on chain-of-thought, I think come partly from this: the trajectory is legible, you can assign reward to it, you can verify intermediate steps. The moment you go latent, you lose that. Your reward signal has to come purely from the final answer, and credit assignment over a long latent trajectory is genuinely hard. People underestimate how much the discreteness is doing for you on the optimization side.

The second thing is scaling and infrastructure. Autoregressive decoding over tokens is something the whole ecosystem is built around. Inference stacks, KV caching, speculative decoding, all of it. Latent recurrence looks really elegant in a paper, but when you try to make it efficient at scale, you end up reinventing a lot of machinery, and the wins often shrink. I've seen so many architectural ideas look great at small scale and then just get washed out when you go to the regimes that actually matter. So my prior on any new mechanism is: show me the scaling curve, not the one-off result.

The third thing is interpretability and trust, which I know people sometimes dismiss, but it's practically important. If a model is doing all its reasoning in continuous space, you have a system that gets to an answer and you have no idea how. For a lot of deployments, that's just not acceptable. The chain-of-thought may not be perfectly faithful, but it's a lot better than nothing.

That said, I don't think it's an either-or. The thing I actually find interesting is hybrid approaches. You can imagine models that do a chunk of latent computation, almost like a scratchpad in hidden space, and then periodically crystallize into tokens. Or things like adaptive depth, where the model decides how much more compute to spend on a given position before emitting anything. In some sense, deeper networks already do latent thinking. Every layer is a reasoning step that never gets verbalized. So the question isn't really latent versus tokens, it's how you allocate compute between the two, and how you train the model to make that allocation well.

So I'd say: I'm genuinely optimistic about the direction long term, I just think the near-term wins are going to come from making the token-based approaches better, and the latent stuff will get folded in gradually rather than replacing anything wholesale.

r002.rationale: It does not address whether model thought must resemble human thought or reject that assumption.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting question is whether language is the right space for every part of reasoning. When we ask a model to think through discrete tokens, we’re asking it to turn every intermediate step into words. That’s useful—you can inspect the steps, and the model can condition on what it’s already written—but it’s also a constraint.

With latent thinking, you let the model do more computation in a continuous representation before producing an answer. In principle, it could carry information that’s difficult or inefficient to express in words. But a continuous representation doesn’t automatically give you better reasoning. You still need a training signal that teaches the model to use that additional computation productively.

So I’d frame it as a question of where you allocate computation. Which steps benefit from being explicit, and which can happen internally? A hybrid seems quite compelling: internal computation for some parts, language for others. The important test is whether that gives you better answers for the same compute budget, rather than simply making the reasoning less visible.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting question is whether every step of reasoning needs to be expressed as a word. With a chain of thought, you’re asking the model to turn its intermediate computation into language, and then consume that language again. That’s useful because language gives you a very strong training signal, but it may not be the most efficient representation for every computation.

With latent thinking, you could let the model do several steps in a continuous representation before producing the next token. Potentially, that gives it more computation without requiring a longer written explanation. But the hard part is learning what to do with those steps. You can’t just give a model extra latent steps and assume that useful reasoning will emerge. You need an objective that makes those steps productive.

So I see it as a promising direction, but not necessarily a replacement for reasoning in language. A hybrid is quite natural: some computation happens internally, and the model uses language when it needs to articulate something, check a result, or interact with the outside world. The important test is whether that actually improves the quality of the answer for the amount of compute you spend.
